Seaward Sands: A handful of empty shells, ridged and chalky. Ground with a stone, about every second handful crumbles into bonemeal for gardens and fields.
Crush the shells into a coarse powder. About half the time there is enough to make Bonemeal.
A whole trunk the river brought down and the tide threw back, bleached and smooth. Hauled clear of the water it is an ordinary log.
Drag the log up out of the wet so it can be carried and worked like any other.
A wide beach of pale sand where the land finally runs out. Gulls work the tideline, and the open sea stretches away to the south and east.
Search the tideline for anything the water left behind.
A stretch of sand where every tide leaves a fresh scatter of shells. Comb it and it fills again given time.
Sift the sand by hand for shells worth keeping.
The tide has not brought more yet
Past the river's mouth the bank gives way to a low shore of shingle and wrack. The sea is close enough to hear, and whatever the river carries down ends up here.
Search the tideline for anything the water left behind.
The river slows and spreads here before it meets the sea, and the water turns brackish. Reeds crowd the mud, and the mosquitoes are as bad as anywhere upstream.
Estuary, Riverbank: Conditions: Brackish water, humid soil. Flora: Reeds. Fauna: Mosquitoes, river fish.
A curve of white sand where the island meets the sea. Palms lean over the beach, and green, broken country rises inland.
Search the tideline for anything the water left behind.

A stony shore under low mist, dark firs crowding down to the water and a weathered driftwood post standing at the waterline with a rope wound round it. Far out to the south-east, on a clear day, there is land.

Push off past the breakers and paddle across the open water to the island. The crossing takes about six hours. It is hard paddling and you arrive wet. Now and then the sea is rough, and in winter storms are common.
Fine white sand slopes gently into clear shallows here, the easiest place on this shore to come in through the surf. Back to the north-west, past the open water, lies the mainland coast.

Run the outrigger back into the surf and paddle home to the mainland beach. The crossing takes about six hours. It is hard paddling and you arrive wet. Now and then the sea is rough, and in winter storms are common.
A narrow dugout canoe lashed by two poles to a slim log float, a paddle laid along its bottom. It carries you across the open water between the mainland coast and the island.
Green water breaking on white sand, warm to the knee. You can wash in it, or hold your breath and dive for what lies on the bottom.
Wade in and scrub off the road, the sweat and the sand.
Hold your breath and feel along the bottom for shells and weed.
A bowl in the rocks the sea left full: crabs in the crevices, prawns in the shallows, weed on the walls. Pick it clean and it slowly restocks.
Turn over the weed and reach into the crevices for crabs and prawns.
The pool is picked clean for now
Glossy green strands off the rocks, salty and a little slick. Edible as it comes, if you do not mind the chew.
Chew the weed as it is.
A palm-sized crab, hard-shelled and quick. The claws hold the meat.
Crack the shell and eat the meat as it is.
A clear-bodied prawn from the shallows of the pool. Little, but sweet.
Peel it and eat it as it is.
A sheltered inlet where the reef breaks the swell. The water lies clear and still over coral and sand, and the tide lays weed and shells along the beach.
Search the tideline for shells, weed and anything else the reef let through.
Clear, warm water over the reef, so still you can see the coral below. You can wash in it, or hold your breath and dive for what lies on the bottom.
Wade in and scrub off the road, the sweat and the sand.
Hold your breath and feel along the bottom for shells and weed.
A shore of dark, weed-hung boulders where the swell breaks white. Pools of trapped seawater sit between the rocks, and far to the east an islet streaked white by gulls stands out of the sea.
Pick over the rocks and pools for shells, flint and anything the swell left wedged between the boulders.

A drowned wood of stilt-rooted trees standing in brown, brackish water. Crabs scuttle over the mud between the roots, and the sea seeps in and out beneath the canopy. Mosquitoes breed in the still water, thickest in summer, and their bites can bring on swamp fever.
Wade among the roots for crabs, sticks and the weed the tide leaves hanging in them.
A long, empty beach of grey sand under a bare headland, littered with sea-worn flint and bleached wood. To the north an islet of white-streaked rock stands off the shore.
Walk the empty tideline for flint, shells and stones.
Where the beach gives way to the jungle: leaning palms, scrub and dry fronds over pale sand. Inland, the green closes in.
Search the scrub at the edge of the trees for sticks, dry leaves and stones.
A little hidden beach walled in by cliffs. The cove is deep and calm, and across the open water to the north-east an islet of white-streaked rock breaks the horizon.
Search the small beach for shells, stones and the odd crab under the weed.
A stack of rock rising sheer from the sea, white with the droppings of the gulls that nest on every ledge. Nothing grows here but salt-crusted grass, and the only way back is to swim.
Climb about the ledges for feathers, shells and stones, keeping clear of the nesting gulls.
Warm water surging in and out between the boulders. You can wash in a sheltered gap between the rocks, or hold your breath and dive along them for what clings there.
Wade in and scrub off the road, the sweat and the sand.
Hold your breath and feel along the rocks for shells, weed and loose stones.
Long grey rollers break on the strand and drag back over flint and shell. You can wash in the shallows, or dive out past the break.
Wade in and scrub off the road, the sweat and the sand.
Swim out past the breaking surf and feel along the bottom for shells, flint and weed.
Brown water, half sea and half rain, lapping among the roots. You can wash in it, or grope along the muddy bottom between the roots.
Wade in and scrub off the road, the sweat and the sand.
Duck under and feel along the muddy bottom between the roots for crabs and weed.
Deep, still water in the cliffs' shadow, clear down to a pale sandy floor. You can wash in it, or dive for what lies on the bottom.
Wade in and scrub off the road, the sweat and the sand.
Hold your breath and search the cove's sandy floor for shells and weed.
Gull Stack stands off the shore across open water, a hard swim away. Swimming there soaks you through and tires you, and you need daylight to see the rocks.
Swim across the open water to Gull Stack. It takes about half an hour and leaves you soaked and tired.
Across the water lies Boulder Shore. Swimming back soaks you through and tires you, and you need daylight to see the rocks.
Swim across the open water to Boulder Shore. It takes about half an hour and leaves you soaked and tired.
Gull Stack stands off the shore across open water, a hard swim away. Swimming there soaks you through and tires you, and you need daylight to see the rocks.
Swim across the open water to Gull Stack. It takes about half an hour and leaves you soaked and tired.
Across the water lies Bleak Strand. Swimming back soaks you through and tires you, and you need daylight to see the rocks.
Swim across the open water to Bleak Strand. It takes about half an hour and leaves you soaked and tired.
Gull Stack stands off the shore across open water, a hard swim away. Swimming there soaks you through and tires you, and you need daylight to see the rocks.
Swim across the open water to Gull Stack. It takes about half an hour and leaves you soaked and tired.
Across the water lies Cliffbound Cove. Swimming back soaks you through and tires you, and you need daylight to see the rocks.
Swim across the open water to Cliffbound Cove. It takes about half an hour and leaves you soaked and tired.
A few steps through the scrub at the top of the beach bring you to Palm Fringe.
Walk through the scrub to Palm Fringe. It is only a few steps.
A few steps through the scrub at the top of the beach bring you to Landfall Strand.
Walk through the scrub to Landfall Strand. It is only a few steps.
A long way round along the shore, over rocks and through mud, to Rootwater Thicket.
Follow the shore the long way round to Rootwater Thicket. It takes about half an hour.
A long way round along the shore, over rocks and through mud, to Coral Inlet.
Follow the shore the long way round to Coral Inlet. It takes about half an hour.
A long way round along the shore, over rocks and through mud, to Bleak Strand.
Follow the shore the long way round to Bleak Strand. It takes about half an hour.
A long way round along the shore, over rocks and through mud, to Rootwater Thicket.
Follow the shore the long way round to Rootwater Thicket. It takes about half an hour.

A dugout canoe hollowed from a tree log, its seams patched with bark. On a flowing river it carries you and your load all the way down to Brackwater Mouth, the river's end, in about an hour. It cannot be paddled upstream, on a lake, a marsh or a frozen river, and it is heavy to carry.
Push off into the current and let the river carry you down to Brackwater Mouth, where it meets the sea. About an hour.
A dugout canoe that paddles you down a flowing river to Brackwater Mouth. Requires a tree log, 2 oak bark and a cutting tool.
Unlocked after obtaining a Tree Log

A tangled wood of vine-hung trees under a close green roof. The light comes down in coins, the air is thick and wet, and every trunk is wrapped in creepers. The sea breeze is a short walk to the west.
Push through the undergrowth for sticks, fibres and stones, and the mud where the roots hold water.
A wide, open plain of tall pale grass, bright after the woods. The wind runs through it in long waves, and the ground rises gently to the south.
Walk the grass for tough fibres, loose stones and the odd stick.
The eastern half of the grassland: knee-high grass dotted with scrub, with a grey beach showing beyond it to the east.
Walk the grass for fibres, stones and dry twigs.

Low ground of standing water, black mud and tall reeds. The air hums with insects, and the way south goes deeper into the trees. A broken rock face rises to the east. The mosquitoes are worst in summer, and their bites can bring on swamp fever.
Wade the edges for mud, reed fibres and sticks.
The wood closed over completely: great trunks, a roof so thick it is dusk at noon, and a floor of leaf mould that gives underfoot. Paths of a kind lead off east and south.
Search the dim forest floor for fallen sticks, fibres and mud.
A high, windswept ridge of broken rock and stunted trees, wrapped in drifting cloud. Cliffs drop away to the west, and the green of the forest lies far below.
Pick over the rock and scrub for stones, flint and sticks.
A small green valley closed in on every side, with a quiet stream and soft ground. Nothing in it has been disturbed for a very long time.
Search the valley floor for stones, sticks, fibres and mud.
Follow the trail inland from the scrub into the jungle. It takes about half an hour.
A trail from the back of the beach into the jungle: a few steps of scrub, then the trees close over.
Follow the trail back out of the jungle to the palms and the sand. It takes about half an hour.
A trail out of the jungle to the beach: the trees thin and the light comes up white.
Scramble up the cliff to Misty Ridge. Skill and good handholds make a fall less likely; a tired climber is sure to fall. It takes about a quarter of an hour.
A steep stony scramble up the cliffs behind the cove to the ridge above. A fall hurts, and a tired climber is sure to fall.
Climb down the cliff to Cliffbound Cove. Skill and good handholds make a fall less likely; a tired climber is sure to fall. It takes about a quarter of an hour.
A steep climb down the cliffs to a hidden cove. A fall hurts, and a tired climber is sure to fall.
Climb the broken rock face up to Misty Ridge. Skill and good handholds make a fall less likely; a tired climber is sure to fall. It takes about a quarter of an hour.
A broken rock face above the marsh, steep but climbable, leads up to the ridge. A fall hurts, and a tired climber is sure to fall.
Climb down the rock face to Reed Marsh. Skill and good handholds make a fall less likely; a tired climber is sure to fall. It takes about a quarter of an hour.
A rock face drops from the ridge to the marsh below. A fall hurts, and a tired climber is sure to fall.
The coconut has gone bad in its husk.
Cut the husk off with a blade or an axe. The husk comes apart into fibre, and the hard nut inside is left.
A coconut still in its thick fibrous husk, heavy as a stone. Cut the husk away with a blade or an axe.
Strike the nut open on its seam. You get the water, the white meat and half the shell to keep as a bowl.
A brown, hard-shelled coconut with the husk off. Strike it open with a hammer, stone or the back of an axe: the water, the meat and a shell bowl are inside.
The clear, faintly sweet water of a fresh coconut, caught in the cracked shell. It does not keep.
White, firm and oily flesh from inside a cracked coconut. Eaten raw it fills and gives a good deal of energy. Boiled in a pot of hot water it goes into the stew.
Half a coconut shell, smoothed inside. It holds a drink, which slowly dries off if left standing.
A long, tough leaf of the palm. Dry, it burns quickly as weak fuel.

Shinny up the trunk and twist a coconut loose. Skill and a climbing aid make a fall less likely; a tired climber is sure to fall, and a fall shakes the nut loose where it is lost. Takes about half an hour.
No coconut is ripe on this palm yet
Chop the palm down. Every nut still in the crown comes down with it, with the fronds, and a shoot will rise from the stump in time. The palm is gone for a month or more.
A tall, leaning palm with a crown of green nuts. Climb it to pick a coconut, or fell it for the lot. The crown slowly bears again.
A palm stump and a few strips of trunk. A green shoot will rise from it in about ten days.
A shoot rises from the palm stump.
A young palm, still waist high. It will grow into a full coconut palm in about a month, unless you cut it for its fronds.
The young palm has grown into a coconut palm.
Cut the young palm down for its fronds. It will not grow back.
Hidden: how many goatfish the sea still holds. Each catch lowers it by 1000 and it regrows 2 a tick; the fuller it is, the likelier a catch.
Hidden: how many parrotfish the sea still holds. Each catch lowers it by 1000 and it regrows 2 a tick; the fuller it is, the likelier a catch.

Hidden: how many sea urchin the sea still holds. Each catch lowers it by 1000 and it regrows 0.5 a tick; the fuller it is, the likelier a catch.
A slim yellow-barred fish that roots along the sand on two chin whiskers. Sweet, mild meat.
Eat the goatfish as it is.
A blunt-headed fish in blue and green, with a hard beak for scraping coral. Firm, white meat.
Eat the parrotfish as it is.
A silver, torpedo-bodied fish of the shallow flats. It fights hard and is full of fine bones, but the meat is good.
Eat the bonefish as it is.
A small shoaling fish, bright as a coin. Oily, and quick to spoil.
Eat the silver herring as it is.
A heavy, thick-lipped fish that lies in the reef shade. A great deal of meat on it.
Eat the reef grouper as it is.
A pale fish of the brackish shallows, with long threads trailing from its fins. Rich and fatty.
Eat the threadfin as it is.
A small fish that crawls out onto the mud and watches you with bulging eyes. More bone than meat.
Eat the mudskipper as it is.
A spiralled shell the size of a fist, with a muscular foot inside. Tough but good when chewed long.
Open the conch and eat what is inside, raw.
A rough, grey shell that opens on a plump, salty oyster.
Open the oyster and eat what is inside, raw.
A black ball of spines. Opened with care, the orange roe inside is rich.
Open the sea urchin and eat what is inside, raw.
A cage of twigs and twine with a funnel mouth. Stake it in the shallows of a calm shore and it catches fish while you are away.
A fish trap staked in the shallows. It springs every few hours; haul it out to take what it holds.
Wade out and lift the trap, with whatever it caught, onto the shore.
A funnel-mouthed cage of twigs and twine for the shallows of a calm shore. Requires 4 twigs and 3 twine.
Cast a line from the shore and wait. What you land depends on this water and on how much of each fish is left in the sea.
Wade into the shallows and spear what swims by. Needs daylight and a steady arm.
Wade out and stake the trap in the shallows. It catches fish on its own while you are away.

Where the jungle gives out, the land climbs into open, rolling hills of short grass and scattered boulders. The wind never stops here, the grass is thinner than the plain's, and to the south a ridge sits wrapped in cloud.
Search the thin grass and the boulders for fibres, stones, flint and sticks.
Higher, drier hills where bare grey stone breaks through the turf. The ground is loose underfoot, and to the south it darkens and a smudge of smoke hangs above the skyline.
Turn over loose stone on the bare hillside for stones, flint and the odd stick.

A black, cracked mountain that steams and ticks in its own heat. The rock underfoot is warm to the touch, the slope shivers now and then, and it is far hotter here than anywhere else on the island. A crater opens on the southern shoulder.
Pick over the cracked black rock for stone and flint.

A bowl in the mountain's shoulder holding a still lake of milky yellow-green water that smells sharply sour. The rim is crusted with pale mineral, the air shimmers with heat from below, and nothing lives in the water.
Search the crusted rim and the muddy edge of the lake for stones, mud and sticks.

A shallow hollow in the hillside where an old wooden ship lies keeled over on dry ground, far from any water. Its ribs are bare, its planking has gone grey and soft, and creeper and moss have taken the rest. Some long-ago voyage ended here.
Search the rotting hull and the creeper around it for sticks, rope fibre and loose stones.

The tumbled walls of an old settlement of mud and wood, roofless and half swallowed by the valley floor. Nobody has lived here for a very long time: only the shape of a hearth and a low doorway remain.
Dig through the fallen walls and the soft ground for mud, stones and old fibre.

The hull of a wooden ship, tipped on its side and open to the sky. The keel is split and the ribs show through the grey planking, and a tree has grown up through the deck. Whatever it carried, and whoever sailed it, is long gone.
A long, rising track leaves the grey beach and climbs across black rock toward the foot of the smoking mountain.
Follow the track inland and up the black slope. It takes about half an hour.
A track winds down the mountain's black flank to a long grey beach.
Follow the track down the slope to the beach. It takes about half an hour.
A trampled gap in the reeds leads up into a hollow in the hillside where something large and wooden lies.
Push through the gap and up into the hollow. It is only a few steps.
The way back out of the hollow, down through the creeper to the reeds.
Climb out of the hollow and down to the marsh. It is only a few steps.
A faint track through the long grass of the vale leads to a low, tumbled wall.
Follow the faint track to the fallen walls. It is only a few steps.
The faint track leads back out of the ruin into the vale.
Follow the track back out into the vale. It is only a few steps.
A low sea cave in the black rocks, its floor wet with every swell that finds its way in. Salt crusts the walls and the air is cold and loud with dripping water.
Pick over the wet rocks at the back of the grotto for stones and what the swell leaves behind.
A low black opening at the foot of the rocks, wet to the lip, leads into a sea cave.
Duck under the lip of the rock into the sea cave. It is only a few steps.
A bright slot of daylight shows the way back out of the grotto.
Follow the light back out onto the rocks. It is only a few steps.
A wet cave on the open coast where the sea runs in and out through a crack in the rock. Its floor is a shallow pool of weed and small creatures. There is no tide to time: it is simply wet.
Wade the shallow pool at the back of the cave for crabs, prawns, weed and urchins.
A crack in the cliff, with the sea running in and out of it, opens into a wet cave.
Wade in through the crack into the cave. It is only a few steps.
The crack of daylight shows the way back out to the strand.
Wade back out through the crack to the strand. It is only a few steps.
A shallow cave in a grassy bank, dry and just deep enough to get out of the wind. Nothing lives here but beetles, and perhaps a lizard that is gone before you look.
Turn over the loose stones and litter at the back of the cave.
A shallow cave opens in the bank at the edge of the plain.
Step into the cave out of the wind. It is only a few steps.
The grass of the plain shows bright at the mouth of the cave.
Step back out of the cave onto the plain. It is only a few steps.
A tall cave in the ridge, its roof black and shifting with sleeping bats. The floor beneath is deep in droppings, and pale crystals crust the walls where they have dripped for years.
Scrape the crystals from the wall and sift the floor under the roost, taking care not to wake the bats.
A tall dark slit in the ridge, with a faint ammonia smell on the air, opens into a cave.
Slip through the slit into the roost, quietly. It is only a few steps.
A grey slit of daylight shows the way back out of the roost.
Slip back out through the slit onto the ridge. It is only a few steps.
A dry hollow among the roots of the ridge where a troop of macaques sleeps and eats. The floor is littered with the leavings of their meals: shells, feathers and gnawed bones.
Pick through the litter on the den floor for anything the troop has left behind.
A hollow among the roots of the ridge, trampled bare and scattered with shells, is the mouth of a den.
Crawl in among the roots to the den. It is only a few steps.
The tangle of roots at the mouth of the den shows the way back out.
Crawl back out through the roots onto the ridge. It is only a few steps.

A cave mouth in the marsh bank that swallows the light a few steps in. The air is cold and still and smells of wet stone; beyond the first bend you cannot see your hands. Bring a lit torch or lantern to work here.
Feel along the walls and the floor by torchlight for what the dark has hidden.
A cave mouth in the marsh bank swallows the light a few steps in.
Go in under the lip of the bank into the dark. It is only a few steps. You will want a light.
A pale patch of daylight marks the way back out of the grotto.
Follow the pale light back out into the marsh. It is only a few steps.
A shaft fallen in on the high ground: a ragged hole in the turf with a floor of rubble a man's height below, and a low opening at its foot that leads further into the hill.
Sort through the rubble at the foot of the shaft for stones and old bones.
A ragged hole in the turf drops away to a rubble floor. A fall hurts, and a tired climber is sure to fall.
Climb down the rough wall of the shaft to the rubble floor. Skill and good handholds make a fall less likely; a tired climber is sure to fall. It takes about a quarter of an hour.
The rough wall of the shaft rises to a ring of daylight. A fall hurts, and a tired climber is sure to fall.
Climb the rough wall of the shaft back up to the uplands. Skill and good handholds make a fall less likely; a tired climber is sure to fall. It takes about a quarter of an hour.
A smooth round tunnel in the black rock, left by a flow of lava long cold. It is dry and dusty, and wide enough to walk upright, and runs into the hill past the reach of daylight.
Break loose stones and flint from the walls of the tube.
A round black tunnel mouth opens in the rock of the uplands, smooth as the inside of a pipe.
Walk into the tunnel out of the wind. It is only a few steps.
A round disc of daylight shows the way back out of the tube.
Walk back out to the uplands. It is only a few steps.
No daylight reaches this deep. Bring a lit torch, lantern or brazier to work here.

A low, wet chamber behind the Black Grotto. Water drips from the roof all day into a clear spring pool in the rock, and the walls shine with it. No daylight reaches here: bring a lit torch or lantern to work.
Search the wet floor and the edge of the pool by torchlight.

A crack between two walls of wet rock that runs on and down, so tight in places that you push your pack ahead of you. Green stains run down one wall. No daylight reaches here: bring a lit torch or lantern to work.
Pick over the rubble on the floor of the crack by torchlight.

A long, low chamber at the bottom of the cave, its floor littered with broken rock and flint. A shaft climbs to the Middle Hall, a squeeze runs off toward the Dripping Hall, and a side opening glitters. No daylight reaches here: bring a lit torch or lantern to work.
Pick over the broken rock on the floor by torchlight.

A high chamber whose walls are crusted with pale crystal that catches any light and throws it back. A copper vein runs through the crystal, and a shaft drops to dark water below. No daylight reaches here: bring a lit torch or lantern to work.
Prise loose what the crystal walls and the floor will give, by torchlight.

A chamber half full of still sea water, reached from Cliffbound Cove by an underwater passage. Crabs and prawns move on the drowned ledges, and a shaft climbs into the rock above. No daylight reaches here: bring a lit torch or lantern to work.
Grope along the drowned ledges and the shingle by torchlight.

A chamber halfway down the cave, joined by shafts to the halls above and below, with a narrow way off into blackness and a copper vein in the wall. No daylight reaches here: bring a lit torch or lantern to work.
Pick over the broken rock on the floor by torchlight.

The highest chamber, a few steps in from the Lava Tube, where the smooth tunnel gives way to broken rock. A shaft drops away into the dark below. No daylight reaches here: bring a lit torch or lantern to work.
Pick over the broken rock on the floor by torchlight.
A small chamber under the Sinkhole, utterly black and silent. A narrow way leads on toward the Middle Hall. No daylight reaches here: bring a lit torch or lantern to work.
Feel over the bare floor by torchlight. There is little here.
A way on through the dark rock to the Dripping Hall.
Feel your way to the Dripping Hall by torchlight. It is only a few steps.
A way back up toward the Black Grotto and the marsh beyond it.
Feel your way to the Black Grotto by torchlight. It is only a few steps.
A way on through the dark rock to the Squeeze. It winds a little way, low and wet.
Feel your way to the Squeeze by torchlight. It takes about a quarter of an hour.
A way on through the dark rock to the Dripping Hall. It winds a little way, low and wet.
Feel your way to the Dripping Hall by torchlight. It takes about a quarter of an hour.
A crack so tight you must crawl it on your belly, pushing your pack ahead. It leads to the Lower Hall. It is slow, filthy and hard on the hands.
Crawl the narrow crack to the Lower Hall. It takes about half an hour, costs 15 stamina, leaves you filthy and scrapes your hands.
A crack so tight you must crawl it on your belly, pushing your pack ahead. It leads to the Squeeze. It is slow, filthy and hard on the hands.
Crawl the narrow crack to the Squeeze. It takes about half an hour, costs 15 stamina, leaves you filthy and scrapes your hands.
A dark opening under the cove's still water leads into the rock. Swimming through soaks you and tires you; the way is short but it is all underwater.
Take a breath and swim down and in through the passage under the rock to the Drowned Hall. It takes about half an hour and leaves you soaked and tired.
The pool's dark water drops to a passage that comes up in Cliffbound Cove. Swimming through soaks you and tires you; the way is short but it is all underwater.
Take a breath and swim down and out through the passage under the rock to Cliffbound Cove. It takes about half an hour and leaves you soaked and tired.
A shaft of wet rock climbs into the dark toward the Glittering Hall. A fall hurts, and a tired climber is sure to fall.
Climb the shaft to the Glittering Hall by torchlight. Skill and good handholds make a fall less likely; a tired climber is sure to fall. It takes about a quarter of an hour.
A shaft of wet rock drops into the dark toward the Drowned Hall. A fall hurts, and a tired climber is sure to fall.

Follow the game trail back east to the Western Wild Woods. It is a long walk, about an hour and a half.

Cut the carcass up with a blade for its meat, hide, bones and antler. It is long work.
Heat soaked up from a hot spring, still in your bones. You feel warmer while it lasts, and it fades over the following hours.
Warm through from the hot spring. You feel the cold far less.
A pool of hot water steaming in a hollow of the rock, with a faint smell of eggs. The snow never lies around it. A soak washes the dirt away and warms you through, though you come out wet.
Strip off and sink into the hot water for half an hour. It washes off the dirt and leaves you warm for hours afterwards, but you climb out wet.
A band of grey-white rock salt in the cliff, crusted where the steam from the spring has wetted it and dried again. Chipped out, it is ordinary salt. The seam is slow to give more once worked.
Chip lumps of rock salt from the seam with a stone. Half an hour of hard work for a little salt.
The seam is worked out for now
A coil of rope with a handful of iron spikes to hammer into cracks in the rock. Carried in your hand it makes every climb safer, and the steepest mountain paths cannot be climbed without it.

A rope and a set of iron spikes for climbing. Raises your Climbing Aid while carried in your hand, and opens the steep paths in the far mountains. Requires a rope, 2 metal nuggets and a hard hammering tool.

The foot of the mountains, north of the forest: a long slope of broken stone below grey cliffs, with snow lying in every hollow. The trees give out here, and above the cliffs the peaks are white all year.
Pick over the loose scree for good stones and flint.
A ledge under the cliffs where steam drifts out of the rock. A hot spring pools here, the snow melts back from it, and a seam of rock salt shows white in the wall above.
Look along the warm, bare rock around the spring.
A high saddle between two peaks, deep in snow and scoured by the wind. Two cave mouths open in the rock on either side: one stained rust-red, one that glints.
Search the wind-scoured rock for loose stones and flint.
A cave at the foot of the cliffs, its walls streaked green. A vein of greenstone runs through the rock, ready for a pickaxe, and green chips lie among the rubble on the floor.
Sift the rubble on the cave floor for stones and loose chips of greenstone.
A cave under the col where water seeps red down the walls and leaves a crust of rust-brown ore behind. Lumps of it break away from the wall and lie dry on the floor.
Gather the dry lumps of rust-brown ore that have broken off the walls.
A cave whose walls glitter in any light. Most of it is only stone, but now and then a round, rough stone turns up that sounds hollow when knocked: a geode, with crystals inside.
Search the glittering rubble for stones, and for the odd geode.
A goat trail leading north out of Fangvale, climbing toward the white peaks beyond the forest.
Follow the trail up out of the forest to the foot of the mountains. A long, steep walk of about an hour and a half.
The goat trail winding back down the scree into the forest at Fangvale.
Follow the trail back down into the forest. About an hour going downhill.
A sheer rock face above the scree, the only way up to the col. It cannot be climbed without rope and pitons, and even with them a fall hurts.
Climb the Cliff to Windgap Col

Climb the cliff to the col, driving pitons and running your rope through them. Needs Rope and Pitons in your hand. Skill and good handholds make a fall less likely; a tired climber is sure to fall. It takes half an hour.
The cliff dropping away to the scree below. Going down needs no gear, but rope and pitons make a fall less likely.
Climb back down the cliff to the scree. Skill, good handholds and rope and pitons in your hand make a fall less likely; a tired climber is sure to fall. It takes half an hour.
A cave opens at the foot of the cliffs, its mouth streaked green.
Step into the cave out of the wind. It is only a few steps.
Daylight and cold air at the cave mouth.
Step back out onto the scree.
A cave mouth on the col, stained rust-red where water runs out of it.
Step into the cave out of the wind. It is only a few steps.
Daylight and the howl of the wind at the cave mouth.
Step back out onto the col.
A cave mouth on the col that glints when the light catches it.
Step into the cave out of the wind. It is only a few steps.
Daylight and the howl of the wind at the cave mouth.
Step back out onto the col.
Where the meltwater off the col runs down into a long, deep inlet between sheer grey walls. Black water, a shingle beach strewn with kelp, and snowfields reaching down to the water's edge.
Search the shingle for stones, kelp and shells.
Walk the snowfield above the shingle, looking for what the cold has left lying there.
A low spit of dark rock at the fjord's mouth, worn smooth and stinking of fish. Seals haul out here to sleep, and the great tusked walrus lie among them.
Pick over the wet rock for kelp, shells and old bones.
Grassy ledges high above the fjord, riddled with burrows. Puffins whirr in and out from dawn to dusk, and the wind never stops.
Edge along the ledges for loose stones, feathers and the odd egg left in a burrow.
Wade into the icy water and scrub yourself clean. It will leave you soaked and shivering.
Sit a while on the rocks and look out over the fjord. Seals come and go, and far out there are sometimes whales.
Far out in the fjord a whale breaks the surface, blows a plume of mist and slides back under.
Round grey heads bob up in the water and watch you back: seals.
Only grey water, ice and the wind.
Deep, black, ice-cold water between the cliffs, too cold to dive in. You can wash in it if you can stand it, or sit and watch it for seals and, far out, whales.
A dead seal, sleek and heavy with blubber. Butcher it with a blade for its meat, fat, hide and bones before it spoils.
Cut the carcass up with a blade for its meat, fat, hide and bones.
A dead walrus, a mountain of wrinkled hide and blubber with two long ivory tusks. Butcher it with a blade for a great deal of meat and fat, its hide, its bones and its tusks before it spoils.
Cut the carcass up with a blade for its meat, fat, hide, bones and tusks. It is long work.
The seal rears up and barks at you.
The seal humps toward the water!
The seal slides off the rocks...
The seal lies still on the rocks.
The seal slips into the water and is gone...
You back away from the seal...
The walrus roars and swings its great tusks.
The walrus heaves itself at you and bites!
The walrus lurches toward the water!
The walrus heaves itself off the rocks...
The walrus drags itself in close.
The walrus slumps on the rocks.
The walrus crashes into the water and sinks from sight...
The puffin flaps its stubby wings at you.
The flurry of wings startles you...
The puffin nips you with its bright beak!
The puffin whirrs its wings to take off!
The puffin lifts off the ledge...
The puffin drops to the ground.
The puffin whirrs away over the fjord...

Wade out and stake the funnel trap in the shallows. It catches the sea's fish on its own while you are away.

Weed, water and loosen the soil around the crop. Keeps it healthy for a day.
A withered, blackened plant. Nothing on it can be saved. A garden plant dies when it is left untended for about ten days, or left in the plot through winter.
Pull up the dead plant to free the plot. Nothing is gained.
The swell got up halfway across. You fought the paddle the rest of the way and came in soaked and spent.
A winter squall caught you on the open water. Spray and sleet came over the side, and you made the beach half frozen and worn out.
The herds have not been back since you last looked

Rootwater Thicket: A brackish tidal swamp. Flora: Seaweed. Fauna: Crabs, Mosquitoes. Mosquitoes breed here, worst in summer, and their bites can bring on swamp fever.
Reed Marsh: A reedy freshwater marsh. Flora: Reeds. Fauna: Mosquitoes. Mosquitoes breed here, worst in summer, and their bites can bring on swamp fever.
Cinchona bark boiled down in a pot to a bitter red-brown liquor. It turns the stomach, but it works against swamp fever far better than chewing the bark. It goes off in about two days.
Preparation: Boil clean water in a cooking pot, then simmer 2 Cinchona Bark in it for an hour. Benefits: Each dose lowers Swamp Fever by 1 but adds Nausea.
Drink a dose of the bitter decoction. Swamp fever eases by one step, and your stomach turns.
Simmer 2 Cinchona Bark for an hour in a cooking pot of freshly boiled water to make a decoction that eases swamp fever. The pot is not used up. Boil the water first: it cools within the hour.
Gut the bonefish with a blade for its meat.
Gut the goatfish with a blade for its meat.
Gut the mudskipper with a blade for its meat.
Gut the parrotfish with a blade for its meat.
Gut the reef grouper with a blade for its meat.
Gut the silver herring with a blade for its meat.
Gut the threadfin with a blade for its meat.
A yam baked whole by the fire until the skin splits and the flesh turns soft and sweet. Filling, but it will not keep long.
The baked yam has burned to a black husk.
The yam is baked soft and sweet.
Sago pith dried hard and pale, so it keeps. Soak it in fresh water to work it into a dough.
The dried sago pith has spoiled.
Work the dried pith into a dough with fresh water.
A grey, sticky dough of soaked sago starch. Bake it by a fire into a flatbread.
A flat, chewy cake of sago starch baked on the fire. Plain, but it fills the belly.
The sago pith has dried hard and pale.
A bowl of green sea water, far too salty to drink. Set it in a lit fire and the water boils away over many hours, leaving a little salt caked in the bowl.
Use: Place the filled bowl in a lit fire and leave it. While it is hot the water slowly boils off (the Drying bar), and when the bowl runs dry it leaves a little Salt. It is not drinkable.
The sea water has boiled dry, leaving salt.
Dip a bowl or other liquid container into the sea and fill it with salt water. Boil it dry in a fire for a little salt; it is not fit to drink.
Start your run on Coral Inlet instead. The reef water, the richest fishing on the island. Takes no time.
Start your run on Boulder Shore instead. Rocks, a tide pool and flint in the forage. Takes no time.
Start your run on Rootwater Thicket instead. A drowned wood. Mosquitoes breed here in summer. Takes no time.
Start your run on Bleak Strand instead. A grey beach far down the coast. Takes no time.
Start your run on Cliffbound Cove instead. A hidden beach under the cliffs, reached by swim or climb. Takes no time.
Start your run on Gull Stack instead. A gull rock off the coast. The only way off is a swim. Takes no time.
For the adventurous: the current carries you to one of the six other island shores, picked at random. Gull Stack is among them. Takes no time.
Start here, on the beach where an outrigger home to the mainland can be built. Takes no time.
The current brought you ashore on Landfall Strand. Start here, land on another island shore, or let the sea decide. Choosing takes no time, and the card is gone once you choose.
Start as a castaway on Far Territory's island, with none of the usual starting stones and kindling. A card in hand lets you pick which shore to start on, or leave it to the sea.
A narrow canoe lashed to a slim float, strong enough to cross the open water back to the mainland. Build it on Homeward Sand at Landfall Strand from 6 Long Sticks and 2 Rope.
Can be researched from the start
